name: Kingdom of Phrygia
info: An Iron Age kingdom of west-central Anatolia centred on Gordium on the Sangarius, which under King Midas dominated most of the peninsula and rivalled Assyria until the Cimmerians destroyed its capital.

facts.predecessor: The western Anatolian subjects of the Hittite Empire; by Greek tradition the Bryges, migrants from the Balkans
facts.successor: The Cimmerians, then Lydia, which took much of Phrygia as its eastern frontier; from the 540s BCE an Achaemenid satrapy ruled from Dascylium

t: Midas, the historical king believed to be the Mita of Assyrian texts, ruled Phrygia at its peak from about 720 BCE to about 695 BCE by Eusebius or 676 BCE by Julius Africanus.
Phrygia fought Assyria from 715 BCE over the Neo-Hittite lands of central Anatolia; an Assyrian inscription of 709 BCE suggests Mita had offered submission and struck a truce.
Excavations at Gordium confirm a violent destruction around 675 BCE, and the so-called Tomb of Midas held a wooden chamber under a vast tumulus with a coffin, furniture and food offerings.
dyk: According to Strabo and others, Midas killed himself by drinking bulls' blood when the Cimmerians overran his kingdom and sacked Gordium.
ev: The kingdom with its capital at Gordium expands into an empire dominating most of central and western Anatolia, bordering Assyria and Urartu.
Midas, the Mita of Assyrian texts, begins his reign over Phrygia at the peak of its power.
Phrygia enters military conflict with Assyria over the Neo-Hittite lands of central Anatolia.
An Assyrian inscription from the reign of Sargon of Assyria names Mita, suggesting Phrygia has offered its submission and struck a truce.
Cimmerian invaders sack Gordium; by Strabo's account Midas drinks bulls' blood and dies.
The destruction of Gordium confirmed by excavation marks the end of the independent kingdom; the Cimmerians remain in western Anatolia.

sections.foundation:
Phrygia occupied the western end of the high Anatolian plateau, an arid land of hot summers and cold winters where olives will not easily grow and the ground is given to grazing and barley. Its heart lay on the Sangarius, the Sakarya, and its tributary the Porsuk, where Dorylaeum near modern Eskişehir and the capital Gordium stood; to the south lay Midas City (Yazılıkaya) and Synnada, and in the south-west the valley of the Maeander with Laodicea and Hierapolis. Greek tradition held that the Phrygians had come from the Balkans, where Herodotus says they were called Bryges. Their language, known from inscriptions at Gordium, was Indo-European and not of the Anatolian family of Hittite; the modern consensus makes Greek its closest relative.

When they arrived is disputed. Some scholars treat the migration as a legend born of a chance likeness of names and place the Phrygians' entry just before or after the collapse of the Hittite Empire at the start of the 12th century BCE, perhaps among the 'Sea Peoples'; others believe they were already settled on the Sakarya in the Late Bronze Age among the Hittites' western subjects. In the Iliad the Phrygians, 'the people of Otreus and godlike Mygdon', fight for Troy from a homeland on the Sangarius. Legend makes Gordias, a farmer acclaimed king when he rode up to the oracle's temple in a cart, the refounder of Gordium, his ox-cart tied to its shaft with the Gordian Knot; his son, adopted in some versions, was the first Midas.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Phrygian economy rested on the plateau's livestock and barley, and in the Iliad the land was famous for its wine and its 'brave and expert' horsemen. Gordium sat on the old trackway through the heart of Anatolia that Darius later remade as the Persian Royal Road from Pessinus to Ancyra, and the historical Midas is reported to have had good relations and close trade ties with the Greeks and to have married an Aeolian Greek princess. Under his rule a system of writing in Phrygian developed and flourished at Gordium, using an alphabet derived from the Phoenician and similar to the Greek, and a distinctive pottery, Polished Ware, appeared.

The kingdom's wealth is clearest in its tombs. The burial popularly called the Tomb of Midas is a wooden structure deeply buried under a vast tumulus, with grave goods, a coffin, furniture and food offerings, now in the Archaeological Museum in Ankara. The Gordium site shows a considerable building programme in the 6th century BCE under Lydian kings including the proverbially rich Croesus, and in Seleucid times Antiochus III settled 2,000 Jewish families from Mesopotamia and Babylon in Lydia and Phrygia with land, tax exemptions and vineyards. The Phrygian cap worn by Paris in Greek art, and by Mithras, survived into modern imagery as the liberty cap of the American and French revolutionaries.
sections.military:
In the 8th century BCE the kingdom at Gordium expanded into an empire dominating most of central and western Anatolia, bordering the larger and more powerful Neo-Assyrian Empire to the south-east and Urartu to the north-east. Its king Midas, named by Strabo, Eusebius and Julius Africanus, is believed to be the Mita of Assyrian texts, king of the Mushki; scholars think the Assyrians called the Phrygians Mushki because they were then campaigning in a joint army with that eastern Anatolian people against Assyria. From 715 BCE Phrygia fought Assyria for control of the Neo-Hittite lands of central Anatolia that Assyria regarded as its own territory. An Assyrian inscription of 709 BCE, in the reign of Sargon of Assyria, mentions Mita and suggests that Phrygia had offered its submission and struck a truce by then.

The kingdom was then overwhelmed by Cimmerian invaders, who sacked and destroyed Gordium; according to Strabo and others Midas committed suicide by drinking bulls' blood. Eusebius ends his reign about 695 BCE and Julius Africanus in 676 BCE, and excavation confirms a violent destruction of Gordium around 675 BCE. The Cimmerians stayed in western Anatolia, tried and failed to encroach on Assyrian territory, and fought Lydia, which expelled them by about 620 BCE and then took much of Phrygia as its eastern frontier, while Assyria absorbed some of the eastern Phrygian lands and the Medes and Persians followed.
sections.governance:
Phrygia was a kingdom whose rulers, Greek sources suggest, drew their authority from the cult of the Mother. In the legend of Midas, adopted by the childless Gordias and taken under the protection of Cybele, a Phrygian king acting as the goddess's visible representative could designate his successor. The Phrygian pantheon, unlike the Hittite and Luwian, was headed by a goddess, Matar Kubeleya, 'Mother of the Mountain Peaks', mistress of wild mountains and their animals, whose priests the Corybantes, 'head-shakers', served her in orgiastic rites of pipe, cymbal and ecstatic dance; her consort was Attis, her sacred mountain Agdistis. Beside her stood the storm god Tiws, the moon god Mas, known to the Greeks as Men, and the goddess Artimis. The oracle of Sabazios, 'Zeus' to the Greeks, at Telmissus named Gordias king.

After the fall of the kingdom the land was governed by others. Lydia made it its eastern frontier; from the 540s BCE, when Cyrus the Great conquered Lydia, it passed to the Achaemenid Empire, and after 521 BCE Darius the Great set up the Phrygian satrapy west of the Halys, with its capital at Dascylium, modern Ergili. Alexander cut the Gordian Knot in the temple of Sabazios at Gordium in 333 BCE; the Celts overran the north, the Attalids of Pergamon took the southern remnant in 188 BCE and Rome inherited it in 133 BCE, splitting it between the provinces of Galatia and Asia and later, under Diocletian, into Phrygia Salutaris and Phrygia Pacatiana.
sections.impact:
Phrygia's lasting gift to the Mediterranean was religious and musical. The cult of Matar Kubeleya spread from central Anatolia to Pisidia and then to the Greco-Roman world as Kybele, Cybele, with Attis beside her. The earliest traditions of Greek music were held to derive from Phrygia through the Greek colonies of Anatolia, among them the Phrygian mode, counted the warlike mode, and the aulos, the reed instrument with two pipes; myth made Orpheus the music tutor of Midas. Greeks tied Phrygian music to the ecstatic rites of Dionysus, Cybele and Sabazios, though recent scholarship finds almost no archaeological evidence that Phrygia was the origin of ecstatic cults and reads the idea as a Greek and Roman invention that made a foreign, 'oriental' Phrygia their symbolic homeland.

Phrygia also entered the imagination of Greece through its kings: Gordias and the Gordian Knot that Alexander cut, Midas of the golden touch, Tantalus of Mount Sipylus, Mygdon who warred with the Amazons, and Hecabe, Priam's Phrygian queen. Under Rome Phrygia held prosperous Jewish communities, with synagogues at Acmonia, Synnada and Hierapolis; Paul and Silas preached there, and in the 2nd century AD the village of Ardabau gave rise to Montanism, 'the Phrygian heresy', with its ecstatic spirituality and women priests and its new Jerusalem at Pepouza.
sections.decline:
The independent kingdom ended in a single catastrophe. Midas, the last independent king of Phrygia, saw his realm overwhelmed by the Cimmerians, who sacked and destroyed Gordium around 695 BCE by one ancient reckoning; the destruction level found by the excavators is dated around 675 BCE. The Cimmerians remained in western Anatolia until Lydia expelled them about 620 BCE, and Phrygia then became a Lydian province and the eastern frontier of Croesus' empire. In the 540s BCE Cyrus the Great's conquest of Lydia made it Persian.

Gordium itself had one more moment, when Alexander passed through in 333 BCE and severed the Gordian Knot; in the chaos after his death Celts overran northern Phrygia, which became Galatia, and the Gauls captured and destroyed the old capital, which disappeared from history. The southern remnant passed to the Attalids of Pergamon in 188 BCE and to Rome in 133 BCE, and the land was divided and redivided as Roman and Byzantine provinces until the Turks overran it after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 and took complete control in the 13th century. Over those centuries the Phrygians became Greek-speaking Christians and merged into the Byzantine state; their language lasted to the 6th century AD. The name Phrygia survived as a territorial designation until the last remnant of Byzantium fell to the Ottomans in 1453, and then passed out of use.

summary: The Kingdom of Phrygia, centred on Gordium on the Sangarius, rose in the 8th century BCE to dominate central and western Anatolia under Midas, fought and then submitted to Assyria, and fell when the Cimmerians sacked Gordium around 695–675 BCE; its cult of Cybele and its musical mode outlived it.
references: Lynn E. Roller, In Search of God the Mother: The Cult of Anatolian Cybele (University of California Press, 1999)
Rodney S. Young, Gordion: A Guide to the Excavations and Museum (Ankara, 1975)

pointDescs.-900: The Phrygians are settled on the Sangarius around Gordium, a people of the plateau's grazing lands whose origins Greek writers traced to the Balkans.
pointDescs.-800: In the 8th century BCE the kingdom at Gordium begins to expand across central and western Anatolia.
pointDescs.-750: Phrygia grows into an empire dominating most of the peninsula, bordering Assyria and Urartu.
pointDescs.-720: Midas, the Mita of Assyrian texts, comes to the throne; Phrygian writing and Polished Ware pottery flourish at Gordium.
pointDescs.-715: Phrygia goes to war with Assyria over the Neo-Hittite lands of central Anatolia, at the peak of its power.
pointDescs.-709: An Assyrian inscription of Sargon's reign names Mita: Phrygia has offered its submission and struck a truce.
pointDescs.-695: Cimmerian invaders sack Gordium; Midas, by Strabo's account, drinks bulls' blood and dies (Eusebius ends his reign c. 695 BCE, Julius Africanus in 676 BCE).
pointDescs.-675: The violent destruction of Gordium confirmed by excavation around 675 BCE closes the independent kingdom; the Cimmerians hold western Anatolia.

notes: The article gives no date for the kingdom's beginning; the register's -900 is the first point, described from the article's account of Phrygian settlement on the Sangarius. The -800 and -750 points both read off 'during the 8th century BC'.
Midas's death: Eusebius c. 695 BC, Julius Africanus 676 BC; the archaeological destruction c. 675 BC. The register's end -675 follows the archaeology.
The saved article has no bibliography; the only work it names is Ramsay's 1911 Britannica article, in its external links.
The register spells the capital Gordion; the article uses Gordium, kept here with Gordion in brackets in the facts.
